about: "Make it specific" prompts for unit-4 (docs/aphug-architecture.md, "Make it specific"); checked by checkJustify in scripts/lib/aphug-exams.mjs.

prompts.title: Describing a stateless nation
prompts.prompt: Describe the Kurds as a stateless nation.
checklist: Says what makes the Kurds a nation
Names the states they live in
Says they have no state of their own, with the autonomous region

earns.answer: The Kurds are a nation of tens of millions of people who share a language and culture and live mainly across parts of Türkiye, Iraq, Iran and Syria, but they have no state of their own; Iraq's Kurdistan Region is autonomous.
earns.why: It says what makes them a nation, where they live and why they are stateless.

misses.answer: The Kurds are a stateless nation in the Middle East.
misses.why: It names the term but describes nothing: no traits, no states.

why.1: Having no shared government is what makes them stateless.
why.2: A currency is not what defines a nation.

why.1: They live across several states.
why.2: Their homeland is in Southwest Asia.

prompts.title: Why a choke point matters
prompts.prompt: Explain why the Strait of Malacca matters to the economies of East Asia.
checklist: Names where the strait is and what it links
Says what passes through it
Explains the effect of a blockage

earns.answer: Much of the oil and goods shipped between the Indian Ocean and East Asia passes through the narrow Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, so a blockage there would delay shipments and raise costs for countries such as China, Japan and South Korea.
earns.why: It locates the strait, says what passes and links a blockage to costs.

misses.answer: The Strait of Malacca is an important choke point in Asia.
misses.why: A label, not an explanation: it never says why the choke point matters.

concept.label: What it links
options: the Indian Ocean and East Asia
the Black Sea and the Mediterranean

why.1: That is the Panama Canal.
why.2: That is the Bosporus.

effect.label: Effect of a blockage
options: lower oil prices in East Asia

why.1: A blockage makes shipping harder, not cheaper.
why.2: So much trade passes that a blockage matters.

prompts.title: Antecedent and superimposed boundaries
prompts.prompt: Compare the 49th parallel between Canada and the United States with many of the borders European powers drew in Africa.
checklist: Names the boundary type for both cases
Says when each was drawn relative to settlement
Says what each did to the people who lived there

earns.answer: The 49th parallel was drawn before most settlers arrived, so it is antecedent and divided few existing communities, whereas many African borders were superimposed by European powers at and after the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, cutting across ethnic groups that already lived there.
earns.why: It names both types and compares when and how each was drawn.

misses.answer: African borders were drawn by Europeans without asking Africans.
misses.why: One side only, with no type named: a compare also speaks of the 49th parallel.

why.1: It is still an active border.
why.2: It follows a line of latitude, not a cultural divide.

why.1: People already lived there.
why.2: They were drawn by European powers, not local groups.

prompts.title: Language and Québec's push for self-rule
prompts.context: Québec held referendums on sovereignty in 1980 and 1995; in 1995 the No side won with about 50.6% of the vote (Elections Québec).
prompts.prompt: Explain the degree to which language explains the push for more self-rule in Québec.
checklist: States the degree first: to a high degree, for example
Ties the French language to Québécois identity
Uses the referendums as evidence and names another factor

earns.answer: To a high degree: Québec's French-speaking majority sees its language as central to its identity, which drove two referendums on sovereignty, and the 1995 vote was lost by about one percentage point; economic and historical grievances also played a part.
earns.why: It states the degree, links language to the movement and weighs another factor.

misses.answer: Québec wants independence because people there speak French.
misses.why: No degree, and it overstates: the referendums failed, so not all of Québec wants independence.

why.1: Language is central to the movement.
why.2: Language was a main driver, not a minor one.

evidence.label: Evidence
options: two referendums, the 1995 one very close

why.1: The No side won both votes.
why.2: Votes were held in 1980 and 1995.

prompts.title: Naming a place: gerrymandering
prompts.context: A student writes: "Politicians sometimes draw district lines to help their party."
prompts.prompt: Rewrite the claim with a real place, a year and what happened.
checklist: Names a real state and its map
Names the court decision and its year
Reports it neutrally, attributing the claim

earns.answer: In North Carolina, the congressional map drawn in 2016 was challenged in court as a partisan gerrymander; in Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the US Supreme Court ruled that federal courts cannot decide such claims, leaving them to states and Congress.
earns.why: It names the place, the year and the ruling, and attributes the claim.

misses.answer: Politicians gerrymander in many US states to win more seats.
misses.why: No place, no year and no case: a reader cannot check it.

why.1: That names no state.
why.2: Too broad to be a place.

outcome.label: What the court decided
options: federal courts cannot decide partisan gerrymandering claims
the map was declared illegal everywhere

why.1: The Court did not strike the map down.
why.2: Districts still exist.

prompts.title: A federal state at two scales
prompts.context: Germany is a federal state of 16 states (Länder).
prompts.prompt: Explain how Germany's federal system makes school rules look different at the national and state scales.
checklist: Says what is set at the national scale
Says what each state sets
Explains the result: differences inside one country

earns.answer: At the national scale, Germany has one constitution, but each of its 16 states sets its own school system and holiday dates, so the length of school and the summer break differ from one state to the next within the same country.
earns.why: It names the national scale and what the states set, and gives the result.

misses.answer: Germany is a federal country, so states have power.
misses.why: It never says what differs or at what scale.

concept.label: Kind of state
options: a loose league of small states

why.1: In a unitary state the center sets school rules.
why.2: Germany is one federal state, not a loose league.

effect.label: Result
options: all states have the same holidays

why.1: Holiday dates differ by state.
why.2: Defense is set nationally.

prompts.title: What an EU membership map hides
prompts.context: A map shades the 27 member states of the European Union, as of 2026.
prompts.prompt: Explain one limitation of this map for showing how much power members have given to the EU.
checklist: Says what the map shows: who belongs
Names a difference it hides, with an example
Explains why that matters for sovereignty

earns.answer: The map shows which states belong, as of 2026, but not how deep their ties are: some members use the euro and some, such as Denmark and Sweden, do not, so states shaded the same may have given up different amounts of sovereignty.
earns.why: It names the gap, gives an example and ties it to sovereignty.

misses.answer: The map might be out of date by the time you read it.
misses.why: Possible, but it names no limit in what the map can show.

limit.label: What it hides
options: how much power each member has pooled

why.1: That is what it shows.
why.2: Location is on the map.

evidence.label: Example
options: some members use the euro and some do not

why.1: Denmark and Sweden do not use the euro.
why.2: Every state has a currency.

prompts.title: Centripetal and centrifugal forces in Belgium
prompts.prompt: Explain how well the idea of centripetal and centrifugal forces fits Belgium, and give one limit of the idea.
checklist: Names a centrifugal force in Belgium
Says what Belgium did in response, with the year
Gives a limit of the idea

earns.answer: It fits Belgium well, because the language divide between Dutch-speaking Flanders and French-speaking Wallonia pushes the regions apart, so in 1993 Belgium became a federal state to manage it; its limit is that it names the forces without measuring how strong each one is.
earns.why: It applies the idea to a named case, gives the response and a limit.

misses.answer: Belgium has centrifugal forces because of language.
misses.why: It names a force but says nothing about fit, response or limit.

why.1: A shared monarchy pulls people together: centripetal.
why.2: A national team is usually centripetal.

limit.label: Limit
options: it does not measure the forces

why.1: It applies to states anywhere.
why.2: Language is one of its main forces.

prompts.title: Reading an independence map legend
prompts.context: A map of Africa shades each country by the decade it became independent: before 1950, the 1950s, the 1960s, the 1970s, and after 1979.
prompts.prompt: Describe what a country in the 1960s class tells you, and what the legend cannot tell you.
checklist: Reads the class: independence between 1960 and 1969
Gives a real example with its year
Says what the class leaves out: the exact year

earns.answer: A country in the 1960s class became independent between 1960 and 1969, the decade when many African states gained independence from European rule, as Nigeria did in 1960; the legend gives the decade, not the exact year or how independence was won.
earns.why: It reads the class, gives an example and says what the legend leaves out.

misses.answer: That country became independent in the 1960s.
misses.why: It restates the class but never says what that means or what the legend leaves out.

why.1: A class is a whole decade.
why.2: That is the first class.

limit.label: What it cannot tell you
options: the exact year and how independence came

why.1: Names are on the map.
why.2: The map is of Africa.

prompts.title: Why islands add sea territory
prompts.prompt: Explain why an inhabited island can add a large area of sea to a state under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
checklist: Names the zone and its width: up to 200 nautical miles
Links the zone to the island's coast
Says what rights the zone gives

earns.answer: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a state can claim an exclusive economic zone of up to 200 nautical miles from its coasts, including an inhabited island's coast, so even a small island can add a large area of fishing and seabed rights.
earns.why: It names the zone and its width, and links the island to the rights.

misses.answer: Islands have their own seas around them.
misses.why: Too vague: no zone, no width and no rights.

concept.label: Zone
options: an exclusive economic zone, up to 200 nautical miles

why.1: The territorial sea is 12 nautical miles.
why.2: A demilitarized zone is a buffer between armies.

effect.label: Rights it gives
options: the right to close the sea to all ships

why.1: Ships keep freedom of navigation in an EEZ.
why.2: An EEZ gives no UN seat.
